title: 0.7 Tuples and unpacking
objectives: Create tuples (including the one-item tuple) and index, slice, and measure them like lists
Return several values from a function as a tuple, such as a (lat, lon) pair
Unpack tuples in assignments and in for loops, and swap two values in one line
Explain immutability and why a fixed record you can't accidentally modify is safer
Choose a tuple for a fixed-size record like (time, lat, lon) and a list for a growable collection

whereYouSawThis.topic: GPS lab: the (latitude, longitude) pair your ROS 2 GPS driver extracts from each $GPGGA fix, and the lat/lon versus x/y ordering that trips up every mapping pipeline

examples.title: Return a (lat, lon) pair, and swap in one line
A track: a list of (time, lat, lon) records
Why immutability helps: a home waypoint nothing can corrupt

predict.question: You try to correct the latitude in a fix record. What happens?
predict.why: Tuples are immutable, like strings: you can't assign to an item. Python raises TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment, and print never runs. To 'change' a record, build a new tuple: fix = (fix[0], 0.0, fix[2]). Index 1 exists, so it isn't an IndexError.

predict.question: You meant to make a one-item tuple holding a satellite count. What does this print?
predict.why: Parentheses alone don't make a tuple; the COMMA does. (8) is just the number 8 inside grouping parentheses, the same as in (2 + 3) * 4. So sats is an int and sats * 2 is 16. A one-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (8,). Then (8,) * 2 would be (8, 8).

predict.question: lat and lon arrived in the wrong order, so you swap them. What does this print?
predict.code:
lat, lon = -71.09, 42.33
lat, lon = lon, lat
print(lat, lon)
predict.why: Python evaluates the WHOLE right side first, packing it into the tuple (42.33, -71.09), and only then unpacks it into lat and lon. So nothing is overwritten too early. '42.33 42.33' is what you'd get if you swapped with two separate lines (lat = lon, then lon = lat), because the first line destroys the old lat before the second can use it.

visualizations.title: Trace: unpacking in a loop, and a one-line swap

props.code:
fixes = [("152305.00", 42.33539, -71.0928), ("152306.00", 42.3354, -71.09282)]
for time, lat, lon in fixes:
    print(time, lat)
lat, lon = -71.0928, 42.33539
lat, lon = lon, lat
print(lat, lon)

visualizations.notice: On each loop pass, all three names (time, lat, lon) change together: one record unpacks into three slots. On the swap line, lat and lon both change in a SINGLE step, because Python built the right-hand tuple before assigning anything.

predictFirst.question: Before you trace: lat, lon = -71.0928, 42.33539 puts the values in the wrong order. After lat, lon = lon, lat runs, what are lat and lon? Does the new lat clobber the old one before lon gets its value?
predictFirst.reveal: lat is 42.33539 and lon is -71.0928. Python evaluates the right side first and packs it into the tuple (42.33539, -71.0928), then unpacks. Nothing gets clobbered, so no temporary variable is needed.

visualizations.title: Trace: a record you can't corrupt

props.code:
home = (42.3372, -71.0928)
lat, lon = home
moved = (lat + 0.001, lon)
print(home)
print(moved)
home[0] = 0.0

visualizations.notice: moved is a brand-new tuple; home never changes. The last line tries to edit home in place and Python refuses with TypeError. That refusal is the point: a waypoint stored as a tuple can't be changed by accident through some other name.

challenge.task: Write fix_record(sentence), which returns a (utc_time, lat, lon) tuple from a GGA sentence (any talker; signed decimal degrees via the provided to_degrees) or None for non-GGA, cut-off, or empty-position input, and bounding_box(records), which returns ((min_lat, min_lon), (max_lat, max_lon)) for a list of records, or None for an empty list.

bug.bugType: lat/lon swapped when unpacking a tuple
bug.report: Field test, Centennial Common: "The robot is parked in the middle of the fenced test area, but inside_fence() reports False every second, so the mission planner refuses to start. position() prints sensible numbers." Find the bug and fix it. position() must keep returning (lat, lon).

explainBack.prompt: In your own words: what does lat, lon = position(sentence) actually do, step by step? Why did writing lon, lat = position(sentence) put the robot 'outside' the fence without any error? And why is a tuple a better container than a list for a single (time, lat, lon) fix?
rubric: Explains that unpacking assigns the tuple's items to the names on the left by POSITION, first to first, second to second
Explains that swapped names give no error because both values are floats; the meaning (which is latitude) only lives in the order, so lat got -71 and failed the range check
Explains that a tuple is immutable and fixed-size, so a record can't be accidentally changed or grown, while a list is meant for a growable collection

challenge: fix_record is your parse_gga from lesson 0.6 with a different output: which fields hold latitude and its hemisphere, and longitude and its hemisphere? What must you check before calling to_degrees? For bounding_box: what's a safe starting value for a running minimum, if 0 might not be in the data at all?

fix_record: strip and split; return None unless it's GGA with at least 15 fields and non-empty lat (field 2) and lon (field 4). Then return a TUPLE of the time text, to_degrees(field 2, field 3), and to_degrees(field 4, field 5), in that order. bounding_box: return None for an empty list; otherwise unpack the FIRST record to start all four running values, then loop with for time, lat, lon in records and update each min and max.

fix_record(sentence): fields = split(strip(sentence), ','); if characters 3 to 6 of fields[0] aren't 'GGA' or there are fewer than 15 fields: return None; if fields[2] or fields[4] is empty: return None; return (fields[1], to_degrees(fields[2], fields[3]), to_degrees(fields[4], fields[5])). bounding_box(records): if records is empty: return None; time, min_lat, min_lon = records[0]; max_lat, max_lon = min_lat, min_lon; for each time, lat, lon in records: update min_lat, max_lat, min_lon, max_lon; return ((min_lat, min_lon), (max_lat, max_lon)).
bug: Print position(parked). Which number is the latitude (about 42) and which is the longitude (about -71)? Now look at the names on the LEFT of the unpacking line in inside_fence.

Unpacking assigns by position: the first item goes to the first name. position() returns latitude first, so the line must be lat, lon = position(sentence). As written, lat gets -71.09, which is never between 42.3350 and 42.3360.
